lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Uncle Tu just turned sixty-two. Social Security: take *fourteen hundred* a month now, or wait until seventy and get *twenty-four hundred eighty*, for life.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: I take it now. Who knows if I'm still here at eighty?

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: Waiting pays almost eighty percent more.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Or take it now, and invest it!

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So we checked, in today's money. By seventy, taking it early has collected a hundred thirty-four thousand dollars. Waiting: zero.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Then the bigger check catches up, a thousand eighty dollars a month. A little past *eighty*, they're even.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Social Security's own table: of a hundred men who reach sixty-two, about *six in ten* live past eighty. For women, about seven in ten.

lines.speaker: L
lines.text: Waiting isn't a bet that you live long. It's insurance, in case you do.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now Minh's idea. Invest every check from sixty-two to seventy. Then use the pile to top up to the big check, until it runs out.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Turned sixty-two in January nineteen ninety: the nineties boom. At ninety-eight, the pile still has about *two hundred thirty-six thousand*.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Turned sixty-two in January two thousand: the dot-com crash, then two thousand eight.

lines.speaker: T
lines.text: I'm almost eighty-six. *The pile is empty.*

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Every start since eighteen seventy-one, fourteen hundred and ten of them: the money lasted to a hundred a little under half the time. About *one in three*, it ran out before ninety.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So the break-even is about eighty, and most people live past it. Investing early is a bet on the market. Waiting buys a check that rises with prices and lasts as long as you do.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: What we assumed: two thousand a month at sixty-seven, in today's money. Single, no taxes, paid in full as promised. Social Security's twenty twenty-three life table. The S and P with dividends. The family are illustrations. The history is real. This is history, not advice.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Would you take it at sixty-two, or wait until seventy? Tell me in the comments.
